strengths: Introduces DOMINO, a much-needed and comprehensive benchmark with 35 tasks, 5 robot embodiments, and hierarchical dynamic complexities (Levels 1-3) targeting the gaps in generalizable dynamic manipulation for VLA models.

Proposes PUMA, an innovative architecture that leverages both historical optical flow for scene-centric historical dynamics and auxiliary world queries for forecasting future object-centric states without adding inference latency.
Comprehensive evaluation of a wide range of state-of-the-art models (including ACT, OpenVLA, RDT, $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, InternVLA, etc.) as baselines.
Offers insightful findings, such as showing that training on dynamic datasets helps models learn robust spatiotemporal features that generalize zero-shot back to static environments.
Demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer on a physical dual-arm PIPER robot platform across 5 dynamic tasks.
weaknesses: The absolute success rate of the proposed PUMA method remains low (17.20% on Level 1 dynamics, and even lower on higher levels), demonstrating that generalizable dynamic manipulation is far from solved.

The simulator utilizes a 'stop-on-contact' simplification to model physical contact (e.g., once contact is detected, the object stops its autonomous motion to reflect the grasping state). This bypasses complex contact dynamics and friction, limiting the physical realism of the benchmark.
In the real-world evaluation, the dynamic objects are pulled by transparent strings, which represents a highly simplified and somewhat artificial way of introducing dynamic motion in the real world.

The proposed training pipeline has high complexity, requiring multiple frozen components (GroundingDINO, SAM2, DINOv2) to generate the target object mask and ground-truth features for the auxiliary predictive queries.

strengths: The paper introduces DOMINO, a highly comprehensive, large-scale (110K+ trajectories) benchmark for generalizable dynamic manipulation featuring 35 tasks, 5 robot embodiments, and 3 difficulty levels, filling a critical gap in VLA research.

The proposed PUMA architecture effectively tackles spatiotemporal reasoning by integrating historical optical flow (to explicitly represent motion) and an auxiliary object-centric future state predictor with zero inference overhead.
Extensive evaluation across multiple VLA baselines clearly demonstrates the difficulty of the benchmark and shows that PUMA achieves a significant performance boost (+6.3% SR) over prior methods.
The authors provide solid sim-to-real validation on a bimanual AgileX Piper setup, demonstrating that the learned dynamic awareness successfully transfers to real hardware.

The analysis of cross-domain transfer (dynamic-to-static and co-training) yields valuable insights, showing that dynamic data helps mitigate static positional biases and fosters robust spatiotemporal representations.
weaknesses: The absolute success rates remain low (e.g., 17.20% for the best model on Level 1), indicating that the benchmark is exceptionally challenging and there is still a massive gap to human-level performance.

The automated dataset generation relies on a simplified kinematic-to-dynamic transition upon gripper contact. While this ensures scalable data collection, it limits the complexity of pre-contact physical interactions (such as sliding, rolling, or aerodynamic disturbances).

The auxiliary prediction pipeline relies on GroundingDINO and SAM2 during training to isolate target objects. For objects with complex visual textures or extreme occlusion, failures in this offline segmentation pipeline could introduce noisy gradients during training.

strengths: High-quality benchmark (DOMINO) addressing a major limitation in existing VLA datasets, which focus almost exclusively on static scenes. It includes 35 diverse tasks, 5 embodiments, and 117K trajectories across hierarchical difficulty levels.

The PUMA model addresses dynamic awareness cleanly by introducing compressed historical optical flow maps to represent dense motion and an auxiliary object-centric future-feature prediction task that acts as a regularizer without adding inference-time overhead.
Rigorous and extensive evaluations against a wide range of state-of-the-art baselines (including OpenVLA, RDT, π0, etc.), with extensive ablation studies in both simulation and the real world.

Well-designed data-generation pipeline utilizing a three-stage spatiotemporal synchronization method (dry-run, kinematic back-calculation, and synchronized execution) to reliably obtain expert demonstrations.
weaknesses: Low absolute success rates: The best model (PUMA) only achieves an average success rate of 17.20% on Level 1 tasks (and significantly lower on Level 2/3 tasks). While this highlights the difficulty of the benchmark, it also indicates that the proposed spatiotemporal modules provide a relatively modest improvement and the task remains largely unsolved.

Simplified real-world evaluation setup: The real-robot experiments reproduce dynamic motion using objects attached to transparent strings pulled by hand or simple mechanisms. This is a highly artificial setup that does not fully capture the physical complexity of real-world dynamic environments (such as complex friction, variable acceleration, or non-linear human interactions).

Computational complexity during training: Supervising the world queries requires running GroundingDINO, SAM2, and DINOv2 on future frames. Although cached, this significantly complicates the data preprocessing and training pipeline.
